Preparing to invest in promising technologies as they are commercialized would provide the advantages of increasing DOW’s energy security while minimizing the risks of technology failure during the development phase. Potential funding sources for such investments include the Office of Strategic Capital, the Defense Innovation Unit, the Strategic Capabilities Office, the Army Futures Command, and the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA), among others. Appendix E provides a list of promising new technologies, and Appendix I details some related NLR resources. Hydrogen and small modular (nuclear) reactors have strong potential for point-of-need generation capabilities. Enhanced geothermal systems (EGS) are less variable than PV and wind resources while also reducing footprints and detectability. EGS use hydraulic fracturing approaches developed for oil and gas to create reservoirs, expanding possible development beyond existing natural geothermal conditions (NLR 2025d). Although EGS systems have high up-front costs, costs are decreasing and are expected to follow a trend similar to costs for PV technologies (Kah and Kleinberg 2025). Technological advancements and reductions in project costs could enable geothermal energy to meet up to 15% of global electricity demand growth by 2050 (IEA 2024a). On a smaller scale, the installation of geothermal heat pumps to heat individual buildings, combined with building envelope improvements, could reduce the need for additional generation capacity, energy storage, and transmission infrastructure compared to other energy solutions (DOE 2023). 6.7 Operational Testing and Pilot Programs While laboratory research provides increasing capabilities to simulate environmental conditions, DOW field-testing support and participation could achieve measurable performance indicators of 22 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. advanced technologies in challenging environments, such as the Arctic. Field-testing of advanced energy technologies in various terrains and simulated contexts (e.g., contested environments, extreme temperature environments, and austere conditions necessitating infrequent system maintenance) can provide valuable insights into performance and reliability. Battery technologies, in particular, benefit from testing across a range of conditions for lifetime, charging speed, and the ability to hold an idle charge. Broad sharing of pilot program lessons learned could inform future decision-making. 6.8 Research Into Emerging Technologies For technologies that are far from commercialization, backing research into advanced energy technologies that address DOW’s specific power, mobility, and security needs could speed progress to the commercialization phase. For example, one interviewee cited quiet alternatives to diesel generators as critical in field operations. Point-of-need generation capabilities, too, are an important area for further research, to avoid some constraints on fuel transportation, reduce risks related to response times, and ensure power for mobile operations. For example, the Defense Innovation Unit is supporting research for SAF (DIU 2023a) and hydrogen (DIU 2024). Research into advanced battery chemistries and designs could expand mobility and power capabilities.
